source: Talmy (1988) Force dynamics in language and cognition (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: Talmy proposed force dynamics as a semantic category: two force entities, the Agonist (in focus) and the Antagonist (opposes it). Each has an intrinsic tendency toward action or rest. The balance is stronger or weaker. The outcome is action or rest. It started in 1981 as a finer split of the traditional causative.
numbers: No numbers; a qualitative diagram system. Example: 'The door cannot open' means the door tends to open but a stronger Antagonist holds it shut. 'The door is closed' is force-dynamically neutral.
limits: Read only through a secondary page; Talmy's own paper (Cognitive Science 12:49-100) returned 403 and was not opened.
agent_relevance: A scaffold can tag each claim with focal entity, opposing entity, tendency, balance and outcome. This gives slots a program can check.

source: Talmy (1988) Force dynamics in language and cognition (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: The two basic steady-state patterns: Agonist stronger gives 'X happened despite Y'. Antagonist stronger gives 'X happened because of Y' (Talmy: extended causation). Causing and letting both come from the balance plus the outcome.
numbers: Patterns only; no experiments.
limits: Secondary summary. Talmy places force dynamics among closed-class grammatical categories (like aspect, mood, evidentiality), so it is a grammar-level concept, not only a word-level one.
agent_relevance: 'Despite' versus 'because of' is a cheap test a checker can run: did the claimed cause overcome a tendency, or add to it?

source: Talmy (1988) Force dynamics in language and cognition (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: Extensions: shifting antagonist (a new force enters over time, e.g. a dam breaks, wind dies down), psychological forces (persuade, urge; 'Herbie did not succeed in persuading Diana to sing another song' has the same diagram as the door), and reflexive splits (in 'Chet was dragging himself instead of walking' will is the Agonist, body the Antagonist).
numbers: Qualitative examples only.
limits: Extension to psychological and social force is asserted by Talmy; the main experimental test of the social extension is Wolff (2007) Exps 5-6 (abstract only, see the Wolff 2007 line).
agent_relevance: The same schema reuses across physical, mental and social forces. An agent could use one push-and-resistance slot for physical and argumentative claims.

source: Goddard (1998) critique and Deane (1996) defence (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: Goddard argued a diagram cannot carry meaning without verbal captions, that Talmy's definition of causation is circular, and that 'force' is semantically obscure. Deane (1996) argued the model is cognitively plausible because people judge force, balance and result through bodily activity.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Secondhand summary; the original Goddard and Deane texts were not opened. The page says the objections are weaker because force dynamics does not claim to be a full semantic description.
agent_relevance: The circularity charge is a warning: 'force' used as a primitive in a prompt gives no check unless it is tied to an observable outcome.

source: Siskind (2001) Grounding the lexical semantics of verbs in visual perception using force dynamics and event logic (JAIR 15:31-90)
finding: First working computer model of force-dynamic verb semantics. Siskind uses 'force dynamics' in a narrower sense than Talmy: support, contact and attachment relations between objects. Verbs like pick up and put down are defined as state changes in these relations (event logic), not as motion profiles. His system LEONARD recognised events in video.
numbers: Test set: five movies for each of seven event types (35 movies): pick up, put down, stack, unstack, move, assemble, disassemble. Camera 320x240 at 30 fps. Six false negatives and no false positives. Four of the six misses were for assemble.
quote: Force dynamics is a term introduced by Talmy (1988) to describe a variety of causal relations
limits: Boolean features; tiny test set; the author says this is a different use of Talmy's term.
agent_relevance: Shows force dynamics can be turned into code-checkable predicates that are robust to surface variation. The same move (judge by change in relations, not surface form) matches our rule that code, not the model, decides.

source: Siskind (2001) JAIR
finding: Motion-profile classifiers fail where force-dynamic ones do not. Pick up from the left and from the right have different motion but the same sequence of support changes. LEONARD also ignored extra blocks, segmented overlapping events in time, and detected non-occurrence of events.
numbers: Four claimed advantages: robustness to motion variance, to extra objects, ability to segment events in time and space, ability to detect non-occurrence. Shown in Figures 26-35 as demonstrations, not a numeric head-to-head.
limits: The comparison with HMM motion-profile systems is argued and illustrated, not run side by side.
agent_relevance: Supports using relation-change checks (what stopped supporting what) as the verification layer, rather than comparing surface text.

source: Wolff and Barbey (2015) Causal reasoning with forces, Front Hum Neurosci 9:1
finding: The force theory (descended from Talmy 1988 via Wolff 2007): each causal relation has an affector force A, a patient force P, a resultant R and an endstate position vector E. CAUSE: patient has no tendency toward the endstate, affector goes against the patient, endstate reached. HELP/ALLOW/ENABLE: tendency yes, concordant, reached. PREVENT: tendency yes, not concordant, not reached.
numbers: Table 3 gives tendency / concordance / endstate approached = No/No/Yes for CAUSE, Yes/Yes/Yes for HELP, Yes/No/No for PREVENT. Example: 'High winds caused the tree to fall': tree has no tendency to fall, wind acts against it, falling occurs.
quote: The patient's tendency for a particular endstate is similar to the Bayesian notion of a prior probability
limits: Theory plus experiments; forces are qualitative (relative magnitude and direction), not exact.
agent_relevance: The most formal usable version of Talmy for an agent: three relations decided by three yes/no questions that code can check.

source: Wolff and Barbey (2015)
finding: Composition rule: the summary configuration takes the affector from the first link, the endstate from the last link, and the patient as the vector sum of all remaining forces. In transmission chains the resultant of link 1 becomes the affector of link 2. In double prevention (A prevents B, B prevents C) the resultant of the second link is computed first and serves as the patient in the first link.
numbers: Nine chain types from CAUSE, ALLOW, PREVENT pairs. Predicted: C/C gives CAUSE, C/P gives PREVENT, A/C gives ALLOW (76%) or CAUSE (24%), P/P gives ALLOW (62%) or CAUSE (38%).
limits: Predicted percentages are model outputs, not observations. The mental model theory predicts PREVENT for P/P.
agent_relevance: Gives a deterministic table for chaining causes, allows and prevents claims. The agent could run it in code when a reasoning chain has several links.

source: Wolff and Barbey (2015) Experiment 1a
finding: Check that the animations show the intended single relations. Eighteen 3D car animations (first or second link of nine chains), forces from a Havok physics engine, cars 5 kg. Participants picked cause, allow, prevent or none.
numbers: N = 24 Emory undergraduates. Modal choices matched intent in 17 of 18 link animations (e.g. A/A first link allow chi2(3)=30.2, p<.0001). C/A first link: cause was modal but not above chance, chi2(3,N=24)=3.25, p=.355.
limits: Small student sample; one-dimensional collisions; forced choice among verbs.
agent_relevance: Shows the three verbs map onto force configurations that people see, not only read.

source: Wolff and Barbey (2015) Experiment 1b
finding: Whole-chain judgments from animations. For every chain type the modal sentence matched the force theory. For double prevention (P/P) people used both 'cause' and 'allow' at equal rates and never 'prevent', as the force theory predicts; the mental model theory predicts PREVENT and missed.
numbers: N = 25 undergraduates. E.g. A/C chain: allow chi2(3)=26.04, p<.0001; C/P chain: prevent chi2(2)=11.56, p=.001. P/P: equal cause/allow split so chi-square could not be computed.
limits: Only the force theory predicted how chains could be built in a simulator; the rivals made similar verb predictions for most cells.
agent_relevance: Double prevention (removing a blocker) is read as cause or allow, not prevent. A checker should not treat 'X prevents the thing that prevents Y' as prevention of Y.

source: Wolff and Barbey (2015) Experiment 2
finding: Replicated Goldvarg and Johnson-Laird (2001) Exp 4 with 16 abstract chains (terms such as obedience, anxiety). All three theories did well on the modal conclusion.
numbers: N = 20. Mental model theory 13 of 16 modal conclusions correct (binomial p<.05); causal model theory and force theory each 14 of 16 (p<.01). With abstract text the modal conclusion for P/P was PREVENT (65%), unlike the animation result.
limits: The force theory does not win; it ties the causal model theory. The P/P result differs between visual and text materials. Authors invoke an atmosphere effect.
agent_relevance: Reasoning from text is not reliably force-like. Do not assume a model reading abstract text applies force reasoning the way humans do with animations.

source: Wolff and Barbey (2015) Experiments 3 and 4
finding: With real causal statements taken from the web, the force theory and causal model theory beat the mental model theory. Exp 4 used chains of three relations.
numbers: Exp 3: 32 compositions; mental model theory 26 right, force theory and causal model theory 30 right each; Friedman chi2(2)=8.00, p=.018. Exp 4 (N=24, 25 three-link compositions, 100 chains): mental model theory 14 of 25 (binomial p=.69, at chance), force theory and causal model theory 23 of 25 (p<.001).
limits: The force theory ties the causal model theory in both. Participants are students; many materials are abstract, so forces are metaphorical.
agent_relevance: If an agent chains three or more causal claims, a table-based composition rule (force or causal-model) matches human conclusions better than pure possibility listing.

source: Wolff (2007) Representing causation, J Exp Psychol Gen 136:82-111 (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Dynamics model, based on Talmy (1988), characterises causation as a pattern of forces and a position vector. It separates cause, enable and prevent, explains causal induction from a single observation, and differs from counterfactual and probabilistic models.
numbers: Six experiments. Exps 1-3: causal judgments depend on several forces, not just one. Exp 4: people compute the resultant of forces by a qualitative decision rule. Exps 5-6: extends to social causation. Stimuli were 3-D animations whose paths came from force vectors in a physics simulator.
limits: Only the abstract was read; sample sizes and effect sizes not recorded. Full text returned 403.
agent_relevance: Source of the claim that Talmy's categories can be tested with controlled stimuli. Needs a full-text read before numbers are quoted.

source: Wolff and Song (2003) Models of causation and the semantics of causal verbs, Cognitive Psychology 47:276-332 (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Compared focal-set models (CAUSE is closer to ENABLE and PREVENT than they are to each other) with a force dynamic model (CAUSE, ENABLE, PREVENT roughly equally similar). Participants sorted and rated causal verbs on the dimensions of both models; the force dynamic model fit better.
numbers: Five experiments; abstract gives no N or effect sizes.
limits: Abstract only. Focal-set theory is the probabilistic rival; the result concerns verb meaning, not causal learning.
agent_relevance: Supports three distinct relations as roughly equidistant concepts. Prompt wording: do not treat 'enable' as a weak 'cause'.

source: Wolff, Barbey and Hausknecht (2010) For want of a nail: how absences cause events, JEP:General (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Force theory account of causation by omission: absences are causal when the removal or non-realisation of an anticipated force leads to an effect, so omission is embedded in a double prevention.
numbers: Three experiments with animations of complex chains involving force removal and virtual forces (anticipated but never realised); a fourth tested synonymy, e.g. 'pain prevents sleep' and 'pain causes lack of sleep'.
limits: Abstract only. Answers the criticism that process theories cannot handle omission.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule for scoring claims that something failed to happen; matters for 'not X caused Y' claims.

source: Khemlani, Bello, Briggs, Harner and Wasylyshyn (2020) Much ado about nothing: the mental representation of omissive relations, Front Psychol 11:609658
finding: Test of the force theory against two rivals on omissive causes. People infer temporal order from omissive causes as from orthodox ones, which the authors say the force theory has no mechanism to explain. Experiment 3 favours the model theory over the contrast hypothesis.
numbers: Exp 1: N=50 MTurk, 12 problems. 'Yes' to cause-before-effect 64% vs effect-before-cause 8% (B=3.85, p<.0001); omissive vs orthodox 35% vs 37% (p=.22). Exp 2: before/after choices did not differ by cause type (43 vs 47% before; p=.09). Exp 3 for 'causes': orthodox A&B listed in 100% of trials, omissive A&B only 47%. Briggs and Khemlani (2019): 66% inferred 'not X causes Z'.
limits: Authors are mental-model theorists; Wolff-camp defenders may dispute. A challenge to the force theory for absence claims, not to Talmy's linguistic categories, which make no timing claim.
agent_relevance: A real challenge for absence claims. A scaffold that checks 'not X caused Y' should not rely on a force reading alone.

source: Khemlani, Barbey and Johnson-Laird (2014) Causal reasoning with mental models, Front Hum Neurosci 8:849
finding: Rival to force dynamics. Core meanings are deterministic sets of possibilities: 'A causes B' means given A, B occurs; 'A enables B' means given A, B is possible. They describe the force dynamics theory as making analogous claims with vectors in iconic models, and say the cause/enable difference cannot be drawn in purely probabilistic accounts.
numbers: Review; draws on Goldvarg and Johnson-Laird (2001). The review text gives no sample counts for the cases read.
limits: A review by proponents of mental models. All three approaches (forces, possibilities, causal models) agree on most cases of causal composition.
agent_relevance: Force, possibility and graph models are interchangeable on most chains, so choose whichever is easiest for code to check.

source: Sloman, Barbey and Hotaling (2009) A causal model theory of the meaning of cause, enable, and prevent, Cognitive Science (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Graph-based rival. 'A causes B' means the causal model has a link A to B. 'A enables B' adds that A is a necessary category for B and an alternative cause exists. 'A prevents B' adds that A reduces the likelihood of B.
numbers: Four experiments in abstract; no figures read.
limits: Abstract only. Wolff and Barbey (2015) found the causal model theory ties the force theory on abstract and real-world chains.
agent_relevance: Another computable definition of the three verbs; compare with the force version when building a check.

source: Gaerdenfors (2020) Events and causal mappings modeled in conceptual spaces, Front Psychol 11:630
finding: Two-vector model of events (Gaerdenfors and Warglien 2012): an event needs at least one force vector and one result vector plus an object. It is close to Wolff's affector (force vector), patient (counterforces) and result. Claims humans think about causation through forces, unlike other animals.
numbers: Cites Goeksun et al. (2013): children aged 3 to 5 succeeded with one-force events but attended less to a second force and used it only when both forces went the same way; older children did better (George et al. 2019).
quote: The two-vector condition : An event must contain at least two vectors and one object
limits: Theory paper; the child data are second-hand here. Proposes robot implementation, not a test.
agent_relevance: A plain geometric formalism (action space, result space, mapping) a program can use, with a developmental note: second-force reasoning is the hard part.

source: Gaerdenfors, Jost and Warglien (2018) From actions to effects: three constraints on event mappings, Front Psychol 9:1391
finding: Adds maths to force-dynamic event models: the map from force vector to result vector should be monotonic (qualitative causal thinking), continuous (action control) and convexity-preserving (generalisation). The authors say Talmy's, Wolff's and Croft's models recognise such a mapping but do not analyse it.
numbers: No new experiment. Convexity: if z lies between x and y, f(z) lies between f(x) and f(y). Talmy's rule noted: counterforces are made explicit only if they prevent or obstruct the expected result, or could and must be overcome.
limits: Pure theory.
agent_relevance: A testable property for any learned 'what happens if I push harder' model: monotonicity and convexity checks.

source: Gaerdenfors and Lombard (2018) Causal cognition, force dynamics and early hunting technologies, Front Psychol 9:87
finding: Argues the main step to advanced human causal cognition is the ability to represent force dynamics. Applies it to hominin tools: hafting stone points to shafts changes the force dynamics of spears.
numbers: Qualitative; maps stages of causal understanding onto tool grades (grade 6 for hafting).
limits: Speculative evolutionary argument. The authors say their use of 'force dynamics' is much broader than Talmy's.
agent_relevance: Background only; shows how far the term has drifted from Talmy's grammar use.

source: Gaerdenfors (2021) Causal reasoning and event cognition as evolutionary determinants of language structure, Entropy 23:843
finding: Extends the force model into a theory of sentence structure: an event representation has two vectors, cause and result, plus agent, patient, instrument and location; declarative sentences express events; verbs carry cause and effect, nouns carry agents and patients.
numbers: Qualitative; compares humans with non-human primates, said to hardly understand external forces.
limits: Theory paper with no new data; strong evolution claims.
agent_relevance: Suggests parsing a claim into roles plus a cause vector and a result vector as a plan step.

source: Wolff and Thorstad (2017) Force dynamics, in Oxford Handbook of Causal Reasoning (cited by Cheung et al. 2026 and Gaerdenfors 2020)
finding: The handbook chapter is the standard review of force dynamics as a process theory of causation. Cited as the canonical statement that causality is transmission of a physical quantity along a pathway.
numbers: No numbers read; only citations of it were opened.
limits: Chapter itself not opened (not reachable).
agent_relevance: Primary reading target for the next pass.

source: Cheung, Qiao, Brown and Lagnado (2026) Attribution of responsibility between agents in a causal chain, Cognitive Science 50:e70280
finding: A 2026 test of process-style views of causation: in an instigator A (hired gun) to executor B to victim chain, four studies (two preregistered) found B held more causal and blameworthy than A. The authors cite force dynamics (Wolff and Thorstad 2017) as a process theory predicting proximal causes weigh more.
numbers: Four studies; B rated more responsible than A in all Study 2 conditions. Intentionality had a larger effect than proximity (Studies 3 and 4). A's high intent reduced blame for B.
limits: Force dynamics is one of several theories discussed; the paper does not test it directly. Sample sizes not recorded.
agent_relevance: When reasoning about responsibility chains, do not assume the first mover gets most of the credit. Proximity and intent both matter.

source: Agent search of Europe PMC for LLM or neural uses of force dynamics (2020-2026)
finding: A Europe PMC search for 'force dynamics' with 'language model', 'LLM' or 'neural' found no paper testing Talmy-style force-dynamic categories in an LLM. Hits were biomechanics or unrelated. One 2026 item on conceptual blending in humans and language models (doi 10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1849083) is a blending study, not force dynamics.
numbers: Zero direct LLM tests found in Europe PMC; arXiv and Semantic Scholar queries were rate limited or returned physics papers.
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search (OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar throttled; WebSearch budget exhausted). Later angles should search arXiv directly.
agent_relevance: Treat force-dynamic prompting of LLMs as untested. Any use in our scaffold is a design choice, mark [D].

source: Wikipedia summary of force dynamics: relation to other theories
finding: Force dynamics has been taken up by Johnson (1987), Pinker (1997) and Jackendoff (1990), and applied to modal verbs (Brandt, Achard, Boye, Vandenberghe), discourse and morphosyntax. Jackendoff proposed reconfiguring some basic notions to fit the syntax of force-dynamic verbs.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Secondary page; no experiments reported.
agent_relevance: Modal verbs (must, can, may) have a force-dynamic reading, so modal wording can be read as force wording.

source: Wolff and Barbey (2015) assumptions: forces are underspecified
finding: The force theory assumes forces are qualitative. Magnitudes are underspecified and often inaccurate but good enough to be adaptive. People may also infer forces that are not present, as when a book closes and the lights go out, or at a magic show.
numbers: Wolff (2007) Exp 4: people compute the resultant by a qualitative decision rule (as cited in the 2015 paper).
limits: By design the theory does not predict exact magnitudes.
agent_relevance: For an agent: ask only for directions and rough relative strength, never precise numbers for the force of a cause.

source: Wolff and Barbey (2015) General discussion: contiguity and hierarchy
finding: Claims: single causal relations need spatial-temporal contiguity, composed relations do not (poison put in a spaceship water tank on Earth kills on Mars). Composition also gives hierarchical causal knowledge and learning by reasoning (overgrazing causes desertification, learned by composing links, not by observing covariation).
numbers: Argued from Exps 1-4; no separate test of the contiguity claim.
limits: Interpretive; the claim that composition explains non-contiguity has no dedicated experiment here.
agent_relevance: Supports chaining small verified causal links into longer claims instead of requiring a direct data check on the long claim.
